title: Pamheiba Changes the Sacred Map
subtitle: How Pamheiba Bent Kingdom, Gods and Memory to His Will
region: Kangla, Bishnupur, Cachar, Tripura and the Irrawaddy frontier
moral: A ruler can change a kingdom, but memory will judge the cost.

sources.citation: Parratt, The Court Chronicle of the Kings of Manipur, Vol. 1 (2005)
sources.note: Primary chronicle edition for Pamheiba's religious and military reign.

sources.citation: Rodney Sebastian, Cultural Fusion in a Religious Dance Drama (2019/2021)
sources.note: Recent analysis of Vaishnavism, cultural fusion and the Puya Meithaba controversy.

sources.citation: Alexander Brandt, 'The Manufactured Past: Meitei Nationalism and the Reconstruction of Manipur's Precolonial History' (2017/2018)
sources.note: Recent source-critical work on late nationalist reconstructions of precolonial history.

panels.shot: low-angle wide of the royal coronation hall, half in shadow, half in temple light

dialogue.text: In the 1700s, King Pamheiba Gharib Niwaz renamed Kangleipak as Manipur, bowed to Vaishnav gods, rode against Ava—and forced a kingdom to choose which past to remember.

panels.shot: slow push-in on Pamheiba seated on the Kangla throne

dialogue.text: When Pamheiba took the Kangla throne, Kangleipak already stood at a crossroads, its old Meitei rites meeting brahmins and Vaishnav stories from the plains.

panels.shot: medium shot, side view of Pamheiba listening intently

dialogue.text: The king listened as Vaishnav teachers spoke of one supreme lord, of bhakti, of new songs and new rules that promised order to a restless land.

panels.shot: low-angle close-up on Pamheiba’s face as he is anointed

dialogue.text: In time, Pamheiba took Vaishnav initiation and the name Gharib Niwaz, letting the new faith flow into the old throne like fresh water into an ancient channel.

panels.shot: wide shot of royal courtyard with courtiers lined up

dialogue.text: The chronicle remembers what followed as royal command: court and nobility pressed to accept Vaishnav rites, old names remade, new food rules proclaimed.

panels.shot: medium shot of Pamheiba addressing a line of courtiers

dialogue.speaker: king_pamheiba_gharib_niwaz
dialogue.text: The king’s faith is the kingdom’s path. Stand with me.

panels.shot: wide shot of a hillside with new temple under construction

dialogue.text: New temples rose in wood and brick, Vaishnav images glowed in oil light, and priests from afar found patronage at the Meitei king’s court.

panels.shot: interior medium shot of a Meitei household shrine

dialogue.text: Yet the court chronicle also tells of pressure, of old Sanamahi shrines disturbed, of house and clan rites strained under the weight of new royal favour.

panels.shot: wide interior shot of palace kitchen and courtyard

dialogue.text: Pamheiba’s orders reached the kitchen and market too: beef forbidden by law, diet reshaped to fit the new Vaishnav ethic.

panels.shot: medium shot of scribes at low desks in a royal library

dialogue.text: Translations flowed. Vaishnav tales and rules were rendered in the Meitei tongue, stitched into the kingdom’s stories through ink and song.

panels.shot: slow push-in on a stack of palm-leaf Puyas beside new manuscripts

dialogue.text: Later memory tells of a great burning of Puyas in this reign. But the surviving chronicles are silent, and many Puyas still endure in archives and homes.

panels.shot: medium shot of two scholars debating over manuscripts

dialogue.text: Modern historians weigh passion against paper, noting the coercive change, yet finding no firm record of a single, ordered libricide in 1729.

panels.shot: epic wide shot of Pamheiba reviewing cavalry on a plain

dialogue.text: While gods and books were reordered at home, Pamheiba hardened his army. Horses were shod, spears balanced, eyes turned toward the Irrawaddy and Ava.

panels.shot: bird’s-eye view of Manipuri cavalry moving through forest toward a river

dialogue.text: From the chronicles we hear of deep raids toward Burmese lands, Manipuri cavalry pushing through forest and river toward the Irrawaddy frontier.

panels.shot: mid-wide of a burning frontier town seen from a distance

dialogue.text: War left its mark on both sides of the hills. Burmese chronicles remember Manipuri incursions; Meitei records speak of glory and captives won far from the Imphal valley.

panels.shot: wide shot of a royal council with map and envoys

dialogue.text: The court watched the wider chessboard—Bishnupur’s plains, Cachar’s hills, Tripura’s forests, the Burmese kingdoms—each neighbour weighing this new, assertive Manipur.

panels.shot: symbolic wide shot of Kangla fort and the valley

dialogue.text: In this mix of conquest and devotion, Pamheiba did more than rule. He tried to redraw the sacred map of his land.

panels.shot: low-angle shot as Pamheiba proclaims the new name

dialogue.text: It was in this reign that Kangleipak took a new name in the records—Manipur—its identity braided tighter to Sanskritic worlds even as older ties endured in homes and hills.

panels.shot: close-up on an elder’s hands touching both Puya and Vaishnav text

dialogue.text: Centuries on, Manipur still carries both traces: Sanamahi hearth and Vaishnav temple, horse-war songs and bhakti dance, all shadowed by Pamheiba’s choice to use royal power to shape belief.

panels.shot: slow pull-back from Manipur’s landscape, valley to hills to distant rivers

dialogue.text: Pamheiba changed laws, gods, even the kingdom’s name, but the record endures as a mirror, asking each age how far a ruler’s will may reach into the soul of a people.
